clue.text: Audio equipment for master class

blocks.note: a head, as in headmaster, is the one in charge
a set is a group of pupils taught together

explanation.surface: A music teacher kits out a masterclass with sound gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of headphones, often with a microphone attached, is worn over the ears to listen to sound.

clue.text: Journalist given chop

blocks.note: first meaning: a writer churning out routine copy for a paper
second meaning: to cut roughly with heavy blows

explanation.surface: A reporter gets the sack.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a jobbing newspaper writer and also means to cut something roughly with an axe or blade.

clue.text: Tartini corrupted (the louse!) by one heretic or another

definitions.note: read with the clue's 'heretic': another heretic

indicators.note: something corrupted has been spoiled and twisted out of its proper form, so the composer's name and its partner get jumbled
by means beside or next to, so the following piece is set alongside the jumble

blocks.note: the Italian violinist and composer, taken as written
a nit is a louse's egg, and also slang for a contemptible person
a follower of Arius, the fourth-century heretic

explanation.surface: A sneering aside about a violinist being led astray by a heretic.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hangs on the run of the clue: 'one heretic' supplies the Arian, and 'or another' is the definition, a second kind of heretic. Arians themselves denied the Trinity, so the two overlap neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone denying the doctrine of the Trinity holds a view the Church condemned, making them a different sort of heretic.

clue.text: Man of faith welcoming male ruler

indicators.note: to welcome is to take a guest inside, so the follower of the faith holds the next piece within

blocks.note: a follower of Sikhism
the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A religious man receives a male ruler as his guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of faith' could be any believer; it is a member of the Sikh religion here, not a priest or monk.
explanation.definitionFit: An Arab chief or the head of a family, tribe or Gulf state is given this title as its leader.

clue.text: Old Marshal storing quiet energy to make a cautious advance

indicators.note: storing means keeping something inside, so the marshal's name holds the quiet sign

blocks.note: Marshal Tito, the former Yugoslav leader
p, piano, is the musical mark for soft
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A wartime leader creeps forward quietly, with energy in reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk on the very ends of the feet is to move forward stealthily and carefully, so as to make no sound.

clue.text: One bitter about ironclad perk

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the pair of words is read back to front
something clad is clothed or covered, so the metal wraps round the rest

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
bitter is a kind of British ale
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron; the word's tail is the wrapping signal

explanation.surface: A grumble about an iron-plated warship being handed out as a bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ironclad' reads as one word, a warship, but splits into iron plus clad. 'Bitter' looks like an adjective but is the British pub ale.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given away at no charge is a free extra, a bonus or fringe benefit of the kind a perk is.

clue.text: Drunken Scottish soldiers vote for abuse to the optically challenged

blocks.note: fou is Scots for drunk
the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a vote in favour

explanation.surface: Tipsy Highland troops vote to taunt anyone wearing glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Taunting playground name for someone wearing spectacles, i.e. an insult hurled at people with poor eyesight.

clue.text: Cut out or included lay

indicators.note: included means taken in, so the little conjunction sits inside the verb for removing

blocks.note: to excise is to remove by cutting
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to snip something from or add it to a layout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' looks like a noun or past tense, but it is the verb used of ghosts: to lay a ghost is to put it to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving out an evil spirit puts it to rest, which is what laying a ghost means.

clue.text: Minor noble about to win common folk with special offers here

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the title's abbreviation goes round the words that follow

blocks.note: Bart is the abbreviation for baronet, the lowest hereditary title
to gain is to win
base as in low-born or vulgar
men are people

explanation.surface: A lesser aristocrat courts the masses with deals.
explanation.walkthrough: BART, the abbreviation for baronet, opens up to hold GAIN, BASE and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A store's lowest floor is traditionally where cut-price goods and bargains are sold cheaply, so discounts are found there.

clue.text: Bug-watching points to magic herb keeping energy up

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from the bottom, so the energy word runs backwards
keeping means holding on to, so the plant wraps round the energy word

blocks.note: E and N, two compass points
taken as written
moly is the magic herb Hermes gave Odysseus against Circe
go means drive or vigour

explanation.surface: A witchy recipe: a herb with an energy boost.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientific study of insects is the field of observing and classifying bugs.

clue.text: Smart girl prompt to take note

indicators.note: to take means to receive inside, so the cue word holds the musical syllable

blocks.note: a cue prompts an actor
ti, the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A clever girl is told to make notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' means attractive and neat here, not clever.
explanation.definitionFit: An attractive young woman is informally called this, and a smart girl is one who is pretty or well turned out.

clue.text: Oaf carrying clout, perhaps - thanks to his wealth?

definitions.text: Oaf carrying clout, perhaps - thanks to his wealth?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests a possible version, so the power word is shuffled into another order
carrying means holding within, so the fool bears the jumble inside him

blocks.note: prat is British slang for a fool
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dim but rich man wields influence only because of his money.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a plutocrat may be a fool who has influence only through riches.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is someone whose power derives from being rich, so the whole clue describes him.

clue.text: Ridiculous token male with unlimited cash is to declare in interest

indicators.note: without a limit means losing a boundary, so the money word drops its end
ridiculous means absurd and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
joins the fodder
cash without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: An absurd token man with endless money is told to declare an interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlimited' here clips only the final limit of cash, leaving CAS. 'In interest' reads as 'an interest'.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert a right to something is to declare one's interest in having it.

clue.text: Ramshackle rendition of "Romeo, Romeo!" by Juliet

blocks.note: surface reading: Juliet's balcony speech performed in a tumbledown way
setter's reading: in the radio alphabet Romeo is R and Juliet is J, so a word built from a J beside a doubled R

explanation.surface: A shoddy amateur performance of Juliet's famous balcony cry.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Juliet are the NATO alphabet's R and J; the answer's first word is built round J and RR.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheaply and badly put together, as a flimsy house thrown up with poor materials is described.

clue.text: Island getting a bit of a battering

indicators.note: a bit of means only part of the next word is used, its letters lying within

blocks.note: the letters sit in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: An island takes a pounding from a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Erin is the poetic old name for Ireland, the island west of Britain.

clue.text: Idiosyncratic boy king first in ring

indicators.note: first tells us the ruler's letter comes before the youngster, not after
in means placed inside, so the pair goes within the bell sound

blocks.note: R for rex, Latin for king
a son is a boy
a peal is a ringing of bells

explanation.surface: A quirky young monarch enters a boxing ring first.
explanation.definitionFit: Peculiar to one particular individual, as an individual's own quirks and habits are.

clue.text: Appropriate celebrity's alias

blocks.note: to appropriate is to steal, nick in British slang
a big name is a famous person

explanation.surface: A fitting stage name for a star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective meaning suitable but is the verb meaning to take.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal or familiar substitute name for someone, used in place of the real one.

clue.text: Smaller group's early years

blocks.note: first meaning: the lesser number in a population
second meaning: the period of life before legal adulthood

explanation.surface: A small band looks back on its youth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the lesser part of a whole and the state of being under age legally.

clue.text: Nasal complaint of the fool in Iris Murdoch's last novel

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the author's surname
novel means new, so the name and letter are made into a new arrangement
in means placed inside, so the fool sits within the shuffled letters

blocks.note: a nit is a silly person
taken as written
the final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A runny nose afflicts a dimwit character in Iris Murdoch's final book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book but signals the shuffle; Murdoch's last book was actually Jackson's Dilemma.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflammation of the mucous membrane in the nose, the medical name for a cold or hay-fever symptom.

clue.text: Report from the Fringe

blocks.note: first meaning: a loud explosive noise
second meaning: hair cut straight across the forehead, in American usage

explanation.surface: A review of a show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes it the Edinburgh arts festival, but a fringe is also hair over the brow.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is the sound of a gun firing; Americans call a straight-cut fringe of hair by this word.

clue.text: Leaks from the second city

blocks.note: B is second, as in B-team or grade B
Leeds, a city in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Secrets get out from Britain's second city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The second city' sounds like Birmingham, but second gives a letter and the city is another.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that leaks lets liquid seep out, as a wound or a pen bleeds.

clue.text: Died in control of explosive mixture

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the death abbreviation goes within the word for command

blocks.note: power is control
d is the abbreviation for died in records

explanation.surface: Someone perished while in charge of a bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunpowder, often just called by this short name, is a blend of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that explodes.

clue.text: Telephone secures new tool pack for seaside attraction

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters of the kit are reordered
secures means holds fast within, so the phone word wraps round the jumble

blocks.note: the blower is old British slang for the telephone
taken as written

explanation.surface: A handyman's phone order of tools for a resort job.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous tall iron landmark on the Lancashire coast at Blackpool, a British resort, modelled on the Eiffel Tower.

clue.text: Tuesday in Paris mostly given over to a drop of Scotch

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the French day loses its final letter
given over suggests turned over, so the remaining letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: mardi is French for Tuesday

explanation.surface: A Paris Tuesday largely spent on whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A small measure of whisky or other spirit, the Scots term for a nip.

clue.text: My turn to pursue musical backing that''s onomatopoeic

indicators.note: to pursue is to follow behind, so the show comes after the first piece
backing means going backwards, so the musical's name is read from the end

blocks.note: 'I'm it', as said in the game of tag when it is your turn to chase
Evita, the Lloyd Webber musical

explanation.surface: A singer's turn comes after the backing track.
explanation.definitionFit: Onomatopoeic words copy the sounds they describe, so they are imitating noises.

clue.text: Uninspiring, beginning to drop behind

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only the opening of the verb is kept

blocks.note: first letter
the rear is the behind

explanation.surface: A dull performer starts to lag behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for dreary, bleak and dismal, lacking anything to lift the spirits.

clue.text: Bid to admit woman to skin treatment centre

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the attempt word takes the name inside it

blocks.note: a bid is an attempt
a woman's name

explanation.surface: An application to let a woman into a beauty clinic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin treatment' suggests facials, but it is animal hides turned into leather.
explanation.definitionFit: A tannery is the works where animal hides are cured and processed into leather.

clue.text: Low-lifers about to go off with small bag

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the riffraff go round the verb for decaying

blocks.note: the lowest of society
to rot is to go bad

explanation.surface: Villains planning to scarper with a small bag of loot.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrotum is the pouch of skin holding the testicles, literally a little sack of skin.
